maths_errors.text: If something costs £92.40 after a 10% discount, the original = £92.40 ÷ 0.90 = £102.67, not £92.40 − 9.24.
maths_errors.correction: £92.40 ÷ 0.90 = £102.666… = £102.67 is correct. The wrong method it warns against is the wrong one. Nobody subtracts to undo a discount: £92.40 − £9.24 = £83.16, which is less than the sale price. The real mistake when reversing a decrease is adding 10% of the new value back on: £92.40 + £9.24 = £101.64, not £102.67. The tip should read 'not £92.40 + £9.24 = £101.64'.

maths_errors.text: To reverse a percentage change (find the original value): divide the new value by the multiplier. Never subtract the percentage from the new value.
maths_errors.correction: The rule only covers reversing an increase. It should say: never add or subtract the percentage of the new value. After a decrease, the tempting error is adding the percentage of the new value back on. Either way, the percentage is of the original value, not the new one.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: interpret fractions and percentages as operators
missing_spec_content.why: Fractions as operators are never taught. The lesson also discourages them: keyFacts[0].examTip says "do not try to do it in your head as a fraction". This contradicts the specification, which treats fraction operators as a valid method.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: interpret percentages and percentage changes as a fraction or a decimal
missing_spec_content.why: Only decimal conversion is taught. Writing a percentage as a fraction (for example 40% = 40/100 = 2/5) is never shown.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: express one quantity as a percentage of another
missing_spec_content.why: There is no teaching of writing A as a percentage of B (A ÷ B × 100). Only the percentage change formula appears, in commonMistakes and keyFacts.
The concept slide claims percentages make comparison easy, but the lesson never shows how to compare two quantities using percentages.
Not mentioned anywhere. Examples would be 150% of a quantity, or an increase multiplier above 2.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: simple interest including in financial mathematics
missing_spec_content.why: Simple interest is not taught at all.

cases_not_modelled.case: percentage increase using a multiplier greater than 1
cases_not_modelled.why: The only worked example is a decrease (multiplier 0.60). No increase is worked through.
Reversing is only described in formulaExplained, commonMistakes and keyFacts. No worked example shows dividing by the multiplier step by step.

cases_not_modelled.case: calculating a percentage change from two values
cases_not_modelled.why: The formula appears only in commonMistakes[2] and keyFacts[3]. No worked example shows it.

cases_not_modelled.case: expressing one quantity as a percentage of another
using a fraction as an operator (e.g. 3/5 of a quantity)
cases_not_modelled.why: No worked example uses a fraction operator.

density.text: Convert the percentage to a decimal multiplier: for an increase of p%, the multiplier is 1 + p/100; for a decrease of p%, it is 1 − p/100. Applying the multiplier in one step is faster and less error-prone than finding the percentage amount separately and then adding or subtracting. To reverse a percentage change, divide by the multiplier instead of multiplying.
density.why: Three ideas are packed into three sentences: the increase multiplier, the decrease multiplier, and reversing. Reversing is stated with no reason and no numerical example, so a first-time learner cannot see why dividing works.

density.text: Reversing a percentage change by subtracting the percentage from the new value — e.g. after a 20% rise the price is £96; student calculates £96 × 0.80 = £76.80 instead of £96 ÷ 1.20 = £80.
density.why: The text says 'subtracting' but the working shows multiplying by 0.80. The student must work out for themselves that ×0.80 is the same as subtracting 20%. It also brings in the 1.20 multiplier without deriving it.

density.text: Subtracting a percentage from the new value gives the wrong answer because the percentage is of the original, not the new value.
density.why: The key reason is given in a single clause, with no numbers. For example: 20% of £80 is £16, but 20% of £96 is £19.20.
It does not explain where 9.24 comes from (10% of £92.40). It also gives no result for the wrong method, so the student cannot compare it with £102.67.

density.text: Expressing things as percentages makes it easy to compare quantities with different sizes: a 30% discount on a £50 shirt and a 30% discount on a £200 coat are calculated the same way, just on different starting values.
density.why: The example shows the same calculation being applied twice, not a comparison of quantities. The sentence claims one idea and illustrates another.
